first_impression.reaction: My daughter sent this, so I'll read it properly. I like that it opens by telling them to see the priest before booking anything. That's the order I'd have told her myself, and it means nobody's trying to sell me a sunset before the basics are sorted.

journey.quote: Before you hold a venue or send a save-the-date, sit down with your parish priest, check that the Church can marry you, and check that your date is open.
journey.reaction: Sensible. Don't put money down until the Church says yes. That's exactly the kind of advice that saves a deposit.

journey.section: If one partner is not Orthodox
journey.quote: The non-Orthodox partner must belong to a Christian denomination the Church accepts, for example Roman Catholic, Anglican, Uniting, Lutheran or Presbyterian.
journey.reaction: Plain and clear. This is the conversation we'd need to have at the kitchen table before anything else, and now I know what to ask.

journey.quote: In many Greek families the wedding sponsor is expected to baptise the first child, so choose with both roles in mind.
journey.reaction: Good point, and one the young ones wouldn't think of. That's the sort of thing that causes a family argument later.

journey.section: Dates when weddings are not held
journey.quote: From 1 to 15 August, for the Dormition of the Theotokos.
journey.reaction: Very useful. If they're thinking of a European summer, half of August is off the table. Glad I know before anyone books flights.

journey.quote: This is the moment for the photographer, and for the people in the front rows. Seat your parents where they can see it.
journey.reaction: That's a lovely touch. Someone has thought about us, not just the couple.

journey.section: How long is a Greek Orthodox wedding?
journey.quote: The length depends on the parish, the priest and how much of the service is sung, so ask your priest for your church's running time.
journey.reaction: Fair enough, but my mother can't stand for long. I'd have liked one line on whether older guests can sit through the service.

journey.section: What are stefana, the Orthodox wedding crowns?
journey.quote: Who buys the stefana is a family conversation. In many Greek families the koumbaros brings them, along with the candles. Agree it early, so no one arrives with a second pair.
journey.reaction: Practical, and it touches on who pays for what without making me feel old-fashioned for wondering.

journey.quote: On Paros, the municipality names Panagia Ekatontapiliani and a string of country chapels as favourite wedding churches, with guests arriving by boat, carriage or on foot with musicians.
journey.reaction: Romantic, but 'on foot' to a country chapel makes me think of hills and steps. Mum uses a walking frame. The page never says whether these chapels or the church steps are manageable for older guests.

journey.quote: Its document steps run in a fixed order: each document except passports needs its own Apostille, then a Greek translation; copies go for approval at least four weeks before the date, approval for the Orthodox wedding coming from the Metropolis; and all documents must be issued within three months of the wedding date.
journey.reaction: I had to read this twice on the iPad. Apostilles, translations, three months, four weeks, all in one sentence. And Greek translation is exactly what worries me. Who checks it's right?

journey.quote: The Embassy does not give legal advice.
journey.reaction: Honest, but a bit unsettling. Then a lawyer is suggested a paragraph later. So who actually walks my daughter through all this if she books with you?

journey.quote: Costa Navarino in the Peloponnese holds religious weddings at the chapel of St Samson or St Eleni.
journey.reaction: By the third resort name I was skimming. My daughter will care; I just want to know which is safe and sensible for the family.

journey.section: Questions to ask the priest and the venue
journey.quote: with the fee agreed in writing before any work begins
journey.reaction: One contact, our time zone, AUD and the fee in writing. That's the line I'll forward to my husband.

journey.section: Plan your Greek Orthodox wedding with Wedded Concierge
journey.quote: One Wedded Advisor plans the venue, travel, vendors and payments with you as a single point of contact, anywhere in the world, and confirms the inclusions in writing before you commit.
journey.reaction: In writing before we commit, again. Good. I'd still want a phone call with a real person before a cent goes anywhere.

unanswered_questions: Can older guests sit during the service, and roughly how long will they be on their feet?
Are the venue chapels and island churches reachable for someone with a walking frame, or is it steps and cobbles?
If we book through Wedded Concierge, who actually handles the apostilles and Greek translations: my daughter, the venue or the Wedded Advisor?
What travel and medical insurance should older relatives have for a wedding in Greece?
Is the deposit protected, and who reads a venue contract written in Greek and in euros?
Who do I ring if something goes wrong at 2am Greek time?
Is the first step a phone call with a real person, before anything is booked or paid?

turn_offs_found.quote: Its document steps run in a fixed order: each document except passports needs its own Apostille, then a Greek translation; copies go for approval at least four weeks before the date, approval for the Orthodox wedding coming from the Metropolis; and all documents must be issued within three months of the wedding date.
turn_offs_found.why: It's one long block with four deadlines and three authorities crammed in. On the iPad I lost my place. If it says 'fixed order', show me the order as numbered steps so I can print it for my husband.

would_share_with: My husband, with the closing paragraph (one Advisor, AUD, fee and inclusions in writing) and the closed dates list
My daughter, with the non-Orthodox partner rules and the koumbaros and godparent point
My sister, who'll travel with Mum, with the Greece section once it says something about access

cta_reaction.quote: Your Wedded Advisor is a single point of contact who plans the venue, travel, vendors and payments around the service your priest confirms, works in your time zone and quotes in AUD, with the fee agreed in writing before any work begins
cta_reaction.why: It ticks most of my boxes: one person, our time zone, AUD and the fee in writing. I'd click once the priest has said yes, and I'd want to know a real person rings us first and helps with the Greek paperwork and getting Mum around.

top_3_changes: Turn the Elounda sentence beginning 'Its document steps run in a fixed order' into a short numbered list (Apostille, Greek translation, approval four weeks ahead, documents issued within three months). It's the densest block on the page and I lost my place on the iPad.

In the Greece venue section, near 'guests arriving by boat, carriage or on foot with musicians', add one plain line that island chapels can mean steps and uneven paths, and that access for older guests is worth confirming with each venue before you commit. Mobility is never mentioned anywhere.

After 'The Embassy does not give legal advice' or in the Wedded Advisor paragraph, say in one sentence who helps with the Greek paperwork and translations in practice, so I'm not left thinking my daughter does it all alone.
